prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

A space-based gravitational microlensing exoplanet survey will provide a statistical census of exoplanets with masses down to 0.1 Earth-masses and orbital separations ranging from 0.5AU to infinity. This includes analogs to all the Solar System's planets except for Mercury, as well as most types of planets predicted by planet formation theories. Such a survey will provide results on the frequency of planets around all types of stars except those with short lifetimes. Close-in planets with separations < 0.5 AU are invisible to a space-based microlensing survey, but these can be found by Kepler. Other methods, including ground-based microlensing, cannot approach the comprehensive statistics on the mass and semi-major axis distribution of extrasolar planets that a space-based microlensing survey will provide. The terrestrial planet sensitivity of a ground-based microlensing survey is limited to the vicinity of the Einstein radius at 2-3 AU, and space-based imaging is needed to identify and determine the mass of the planetary host stars for the vast majority of planets discovered by microlensing. Thus, a space-based microlensing survey is likely to be the only way to gain a comprehensive understanding of the nature of planetary systems, which is needed to understand planet formation and habitability. The proposed Microlensing Planet Finder (MPF) mission is an example of a space-based microlensing survey that can accomplish these objectives with proven technology and a cost that fits comfortably under the NASA Discovery Program cost cap.

A space-based gravitational microlensing exoplanet survey would provide a statistical census of exoplanets with masses as low as 0.1 Earth masses and orbital separations ranging from 0.5 AU to infinity. A gravitational microlensing survey conducted from space would produce a statistical inventory of exoplanets as small as 0.1 Earth masses, spanning orbital distances from 0.5 AU outward to unbound separations. Its reach would include counterparts to every planet in the Solar System other than Mercury, along with most planetary categories anticipated by formation models. It would also measure how commonly planets occur around nearly every class of star, excluding only stars with brief lifespans.

Because space-based microlensing cannot detect planets orbiting within 0.5 AU of their stars, those close-in worlds would instead be accessible to Kepler. No other technique, including ground-based microlensing, can match the broad statistical picture of exoplanet mass and semimajor-axis distributions that a space microlensing mission could deliver. From the ground, sensitivity to terrestrial-mass planets is largely confined to the region near the Einstein radius, approximately 2–3 AU. Moreover, for most microlensing discoveries, observations from space are required to identify the host stars and measure their masses.

Consequently, a space-based microlensing program may be the only means of developing a comprehensive view of planetary-system characteristics—knowledge essential to understanding both planet formation and habitability. The proposed Microlensing Planet Finder (MPF) illustrates a mission capable of meeting these goals with established technology while remaining comfortably below the NASA Discovery Program’s cost ceiling.
outputs.L3:
A space-based gravitational microlensing survey could provide a remarkably complete census of exoplanets. By continuously monitoring dense fields of stars, such a mission could detect planets with masses as low as about 0.1 Earth masses at orbital separations ranging from roughly 0.5 astronomical units (AU) to effectively unlimited distances. This sensitivity would include planets on very wide orbits and potentially even free-floating planets that are no longer gravitationally bound to a host star.

Such a survey would be capable of detecting analogs of every planet in the Solar System except Mercury, whose tight orbit lies below microlensing’s practical separation limit. Because microlensing does not depend strongly on the brightness of the planetary host, it could also measure the frequency of planets around nearly all long-lived stellar types, including faint, low-mass stars that are difficult to study with many other detection methods.

Microlensing would complement transit missions such as Kepler. Planets orbiting within approximately 0.5 AU are generally inaccessible to microlensing, whereas transit surveys are particularly effective at finding planets on short-period, close-in orbits. Together, the two techniques could therefore probe planetary systems across a much broader range of orbital separations than either method alone.

Ground-based microlensing surveys can detect terrestrial-mass planets, but their greatest sensitivity is generally concentrated near projected separations of about 2–3 AU. Atmospheric limitations and stellar crowding also make it difficult to resolve the source and lens stars. Space-based imaging is therefore essential for identifying and characterizing most planetary host stars, allowing their masses and distances—and consequently the masses and orbital properties of their planets—to be measured more accurately.

The proposed Microlensing Planet Finder would use these advantages to determine comprehensive statistical distributions of planet masses and orbital separations. Relying on established observational and spacecraft technologies, the mission was envisioned as capable of achieving these goals within the cost constraints of NASA’s Discovery Program.
outputs.L4:
A space-based gravitational microlensing survey, such as the proposed Microlensing Planet Finder, would provide a broad census of planetary systems throughout the Milky Way. Gravitational microlensing occurs when a foreground star passes nearly in front of a more distant background star. The gravity of the foreground star temporarily magnifies the background star’s light, while planets orbiting the foreground star can produce brief, recognizable deviations in the resulting light curve. By continuously monitoring millions of stars in dense Galactic fields, a dedicated mission could detect these planetary signals over a wide range of host-star masses, orbital separations, and planetary masses.

Such a survey would be sensitive to planets as small as roughly 0.1 Earth masses at orbital distances of about 0.5 astronomical units and beyond. It could detect analogs of Earth, Mars, the Solar System’s giant planets, and colder bodies that are difficult to find with other techniques. Microlensing can also reveal planets around faint, low-mass stars and stellar remnants, as well as planets on very wide orbits or possibly moving through space without a detectable host. Because the method depends primarily on gravity rather than on light from the planet or host star, it is capable of probing planetary populations that are inaccessible to conventional radial-velocity, transit, or direct-imaging surveys.

This capability would strongly complement transit missions such as Kepler, whose greatest sensitivity is to planets with relatively short orbital periods and small orbital separations. Transit surveys have transformed knowledge of close-in planetary systems, but the probability of observing a transit declines with increasing distance from the host star, and detecting long-period planets requires observations spanning many years. Microlensing, in contrast, is naturally sensitive to planets near and beyond the region where they formed, including worlds outside the snow line. Combining the results of transit and microlensing surveys would therefore make it possible to trace planetary populations from hot, close-in orbits to cold, distant regions resembling the outer Solar System.

Observations from space are especially important for achieving this goal. Stable, high-resolution imaging above Earth’s atmosphere would allow the mission to separate crowded stellar images, measure subtle changes in brightness with high precision, and detect the short perturbations produced by low-mass planets. Space-based images obtained during and after an event could also identify the lens star and measure its light or its motion relative to the background source. These measurements would help determine the host star’s properties and convert microlensing observables into estimates of the planet’s mass and orbital separation, rather than yielding detections with poorly constrained physical characteristics.

The resulting catalog would provide statistically robust measurements of how frequently planets occur as functions of mass, orbital distance, host-star type, and Galactic environment. It would show whether systems resembling our own are common, how often low-mass planets form beyond the snow line, and how planetary architectures vary around different kinds of stars. The survey could also test theories of core accretion, planetary migration, dynamical scattering, and the formation or ejection of free-floating planets.

By extending the planetary census across nearly the full range of stellar and planetary types, a space-based microlensing mission would address fundamental questions about planet formation and the conditions that may support habitable worlds. Its measurements would place the inner planetary populations discovered by transit surveys into a much broader context and help determine how typical—or unusual—the Solar System may be. Because the mission would rely on established gravitational-lensing physics, proven detector systems, and well-developed space-imaging technology, it could achieve these goals through a technically mature and comparatively cost-effective approach.

counterfactuals.prompt: Explain the scientific case for a space-based gravitational microlensing exoplanet survey, including its sensitivity, advantages over ground-based surveys, and complementarity with Kepler.
counterfactuals.output:
A space-based gravitational microlensing survey—such as the microlensing program planned for NASA’s **Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope**—would provide a statistical census of planetary systems in a region of parameter space largely inaccessible to other techniques.

## How microlensing detects planets

Microlensing occurs when a foreground star passes nearly in front of a more distant source star. The foreground star’s gravity magnifies the source for days to months. A planet orbiting the lens star produces a short perturbation, typically lasting hours to days, in the otherwise smooth magnification curve.

The signal depends primarily on the planet-to-star mass ratio and projected separation in units of the Einstein radius. It does not depend strongly on the planet’s luminosity or on the light received from its host star.

## Scientific sensitivity

A large space survey toward the dense Galactic bulge could detect:

- Planets from roughly Mars mass to gas-giant mass, with the precise threshold depending on cadence, source brightness, and event geometry.
- Planets at projected separations of about 1–10 AU for typical lenses, with peak sensitivity near the host star’s Einstein ring—usually a few AU.
- Some planets at smaller separations through high-magnification events.
- Wide-orbit planets and potentially unbound, “free-floating” planets, whose short isolated lensing events reveal objects that need not transit or appreciably perturb a host star.
- Planets orbiting faint stars and stellar remnants, including hosts that are difficult to study with radial velocities or direct imaging.

Microlensing therefore measures the distribution of planet-to-star mass ratio and separation beyond the snow line. With host-star detections, finite-source effects, microlens parallax, and high-resolution follow-up, many events can also yield or constrain physical planet masses, orbital separations, and Galactic locations.

Its principal product is statistical: the frequency of planets as a function of mass, separation, and host environment. This directly tests models in which planetary cores form efficiently near or beyond the snow line and either accrete gas, remain as ice-rich low-mass planets, migrate inward, or are scattered and ejected.

## Why conduct the survey from space?

Ground-based microlensing surveys are scientifically productive, but observations toward the Galactic bulge face severe crowding, atmospheric variability, weather, and day–night interruptions. Space observations offer several advantages:

1. **Sharper angular resolution**  
   A stable diffraction-limited point-spread function greatly reduces blending in dense bulge fields. More source stars can be monitored accurately, including faint main-sequence stars that are especially useful for detecting low-mass planets.

2. **Higher and more stable photometric precision**  
   The absence of atmospheric seeing, extinction fluctuations, and scintillation makes short, low-amplitude planetary perturbations easier to recognize and characterize.

3. **Nearly continuous cadence**  
   Planetary anomalies can last only a few hours. Continuous, uniform monitoring reduces the probability that they are lost to daylight, weather, or poor seeing and improves sensitivity to terrestrial-mass and free-floating planets.

4. **Near-infrared access to obscured fields**  
   Observing in the infrared allows the survey to monitor dense regions of the Galactic bulge hidden by dust at visible wavelengths. These fields provide very high event rates.

5. **Better host and lens characterization**  
   Space-based images can separate the lens from unrelated blended light more effectively. As the lens and source move apart after an event, later high-resolution observations may detect the lens star and measure its flux and relative proper motion, helping determine the host and planet masses.

6. **Space–ground parallax**  
   Simultaneous observations from Earth and a distant spacecraft view an event from different positions. The resulting microlens parallax can break important degeneracies and improve mass and distance estimates.

The main limitations remain that microlensing events are usually one-time alignments, most planets are too distant for routine follow-up, and individual masses are not always uniquely determined. The strength of the method is therefore a well-calibrated population census rather than repeated characterization of every system.

## Complementarity with Kepler

Kepler’s transit survey was most sensitive to planets with relatively short orbital periods, especially systems inside roughly 1 AU. It established that close-in planets—particularly super-Earths and sub-Neptunes—are common and measured their radii and period distribution with extraordinary precision. However, the probability of transit decreases with orbital distance, and only a small fraction of long-period planets transit more than once during a finite mission.

Microlensing complements Kepler in several ways:

| Kepler transits | Space microlensing |
|---|---|
| Most sensitive to close-in, short-period planets | Most sensitive to planets near and beyond the snow line |
| Measures planet radius | Primarily measures mass ratio; often constrains mass |
| Requires favorable orbital alignment and repeated transits | Requires a chance lensing alignment but not a favorable planetary orbital inclination |
| Surveys mostly nearby disk stars | Probes planets across much of the Galactic disk and bulge |
| Limited sensitivity to free-floating planets | Can detect isolated planetary-mass lenses |
| Strong census inside roughly 1 AU | Strong census at roughly 1–10 AU and beyond |

Together, the methods can map planetary systems from hot inner orbits to cold outer regions. Kepler constrains the population of close-in planets after migration and dynamical evolution, while microlensing measures the colder population nearer its likely formation zones. Comparing the two distributions tests how efficiently planets form beyond the snow line, how often they migrate inward, how architectures depend on host mass and Galactic environment, and how frequently dynamical interactions place planets on wide or unbound orbits.

Thus, the central scientific case is not merely to add more exoplanets, but to complete the demographic map needed for a general theory of planet formation and evolution.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: How could a space-based microlensing mission provide a comprehensive statistical census of planetary systems, and what ranges of planet mass and orbital separation would it detect?
counterfactuals.output:
A space-based microlensing survey would repeatedly image tens to hundreds of millions of stars in the crowded Galactic bulge with high angular resolution and minute-scale cadence. When a foreground star lenses a background star, any planet orbiting the lens produces a brief deviation from the otherwise smooth microlensing light curve. The deviation measures the planet-to-star mass ratio and projected separation; parallax, finite-source effects, astrometric shifts, and detection of light from the host can often provide absolute masses and distances.

Because microlensing does not depend on light from the planet or host, the survey would sample planets around a wide range of Galactic stars—including faint M dwarfs—and detect unbound planets as isolated short events. Thousands of detections would yield occurrence rates versus planet mass, separation, host type, and Galactic environment, including systems resembling the outer Solar System.

Typical projected sensitivity would be:

- **Planet mass:** roughly **0.1 Earth mass (about Mars mass)** up to many Jupiter masses  
- **Orbital separation:** about **0.5 AU to 10 AU or more**, with sensitivity extending to very wide-orbit planets  
- **Free-floating planets:** potentially down to roughly Mars–Earth mass, depending on cadence and survey design  

Thus, such a mission would complement transit surveys—which are strongest for close-in planets—by providing a statistical census primarily beyond the snow line, covering most Solar-System-like orbital scales except the innermost region.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Compare space-based microlensing with Kepler and ground-based microlensing for detecting exoplanets, identifying the limitations and strengths of each method.
counterfactuals.output:
The three approaches probe complementary parts of exoplanet parameter space.

| Method | Main strengths | Main limitations |
|---|---|---|
| **Space-based microlensing** | No atmospheric seeing; stable, nearly continuous monitoring; resolves crowded Galactic-bulge fields better than ground surveys; detects low-mass planets, planets beyond the snow line, wide-orbit planets, and potentially free-floating planets. Simultaneous observations from Earth and a distant spacecraft can measure **microlens parallax**, helping determine planet and host masses and distances. | Microlensing events are rare and normally do not repeat, making confirmation and follow-up difficult. Planet properties can remain degenerate unless parallax, finite-source effects, or lens light are measured. Requires high cadence over very dense fields and is limited by mission lifetime, telemetry, and field accessibility. |
| **Kepler transit survey** | Extremely precise, continuous photometry; produced large, statistically uniform samples; especially effective for measuring planet radii and occurrence rates for short- to moderate-period planets. Multiple transits reveal orbital periods and multiplanet architectures. | Requires nearly edge-on orbits and repeated transits, so sensitivity falls for wide-orbit planets. It measures radius rather than mass; RV or transit-timing follow-up is often needed. False positives, stellar-radius uncertainties, and reduced sensitivity around faint or active stars are important. Kepler was not designed primarily for crowded-field microlensing. |
| **Ground-based microlensing** | Relatively inexpensive and flexible; networks of telescopes provide long time coverage and rapid follow-up. Sensitive to planets around distant and faint stars, particularly cool planets near or beyond the snow line, and does not depend strongly on host-star brightness. Can detect very low-mass or unbound planets through short perturbations. | Atmospheric seeing, weather, daylight, and crowding reduce precision and create gaps; short planetary anomalies may be missed. Ground observations alone often suffer from degeneracies in lens mass and distance. Lower angular resolution also makes measurement of lens light and later separation of lens and source more difficult. |

### Kepler specifically as a microlensing platform

Although Kepler was primarily a transit mission, **K2 Campaign 9** observed Galactic-bulge microlensing events simultaneously with ground surveys. The large Earth–Kepler separation allowed measurement of the same event from two viewpoints, providing microlens parallax and better constraints on lens masses and distances.

Its limitations for this role included:

- A crowded bulge field and Kepler’s relatively large pixels  
- Reduced pointing stability during the K2 mission  
- A limited observing window and fixed field  
- Difficulty extracting precise light curves for faint, blended stars  

### Overall comparison

- **Kepler transits:** best for radii, periods, and population statistics of relatively close-in planets.  
- **Ground microlensing:** strong for discovering cold, distant, and low-mass planets at modest cost, but affected by atmosphere and parameter degeneracies.  
- **Dedicated space microlensing:** combines sensitivity to cold and free-floating planets with better angular resolution and continuity; when paired with ground observations, it can also provide substantially better mass and distance measurements. Its main disadvantages are cost and the intrinsically nonrepeatable nature of microlensing events.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize why the proposed Microlensing Planet Finder is important for understanding planet formation and habitability, mentioning host-star characterization, terrestrial-planet sensitivity, technological readiness, and cost.
counterfactuals.output:
The proposed **Microlensing Planet Finder (MPF)** would provide a statistical census of planetary systems in a region largely inaccessible to transit and radial-velocity surveys—especially beyond the snow line, where planet formation is expected to be most efficient. It would:

- **Characterize host stars:** Space-based imaging could detect light from most lens stars and measure their masses, distances, and relative motions, allowing planet masses and orbital separations to be determined rather than merely mass ratios.
- **Detect terrestrial planets:** MPF would be sensitive to Earth-mass—and in favorable cases sub-Earth-mass—planets over a broad range of separations, including habitable-zone planets around lower-mass stars, cold terrestrial planets, and free-floating worlds.
- **Test formation and habitability models:** By measuring how common rocky planets, gas giants, and system architectures are across stellar types and orbital distances, it would constrain core-accretion, migration, and the conditions that produce potentially habitable systems.
- **Use mature technology:** The mission relied largely on proven telescope, spacecraft, detector, and microlensing-analysis technologies, requiring no major technological breakthroughs.
- **Remain comparatively affordable:** It was conceived as a focused, moderate-cost mission—roughly in the few-hundred-million-dollar class—capable of delivering a broad planetary census at substantially lower cost than a large flagship observatory.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
